subject: Medical Terminology
title: Lecture 14 and 15 - Blood and Lymphatic System

A.q: Blood is classed as a specialized connective tissue. Which description of its composition is correct?
options: The liquid portion is serum, and the formed cellular portion consists of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.
The liquid portion is lymph, and the formed cellular portion consists of megakaryocytes, fibroblasts, and osteocytes.
The liquid portion is plasma, and the formed cellular portion consists of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes.
The liquid portion is plasma, and the formed cellular portion consists of lymphocytes, monocytes, and platelets.
A.explain: Blood is a fluid connective tissue whose liquid part is plasma and whose cellular part is erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. Serum is the post-clotting fluid and is not the living liquid matrix of circulating blood. Lymph belongs to the lymphatic system, and megakaryocytes, fibroblasts, and osteocytes are marrow and connective-tissue cells rather than the circulating formed elements. Lymphocytes, monocytes, and platelets omit the red cells and the granulocyte class, so that list is not the full cellular composition.

A.q: Which set of duties belongs to the lymphatic system rather than to blood itself?
options: Filtering foreign particles from lymph, sustaining lymphocyte responses, balancing tissue fluid, and absorbing dietary fats.
Delivering oxygen and nutrients to cells, conveying hormones to their targets, and removing carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes.
Generating the pressure that drives flow, opening and closing its own valves, and perfusing the heart muscle through coronary vessels.
Producing red cells, white cells, and platelets, storing calcium salts, and giving attachment to skeletal muscle.
A.explain: The lymphatic system filters microorganisms and foreign particles out of lymph, supports lymphocyte activity during immune responses, maintains the internal fluid environment between capillaries and tissue cells, and carries fats away from the digestive system. Delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing carbon dioxide and wastes is the transport work of blood. Generating flow pressure and opening valves describes the heart and its vessels. Producing blood cells, storing minerals, and giving muscle attachment are skeletal and marrow roles.

A.q: Plasma and serum are both liquid fractions of blood. Which statement about them is correct?
options: Serum contains the clotting factors, whereas plasma is the fluid that remains after the blood has clotted.
Both plasma and serum lack clotting factors and differ only in whether red cells are suspended in them.
Plasma is the post-clotting fluid, and serum is the fluid that still holds fibrinogen and the other factors.
Plasma holds the clotting factors such as fibrinogen, and serum is the fluid left after clotting, without those factors.
A.explain: Plasma is the clear yellowish fluid that still carries the clotting factors, including fibrinogen, and serum is what remains once clotting has consumed those factors. Serum contains the clotting factors, whereas plasma is the fluid that remains after the blood has clotted, reverses the pair. Both plasma and serum lack clotting factors and differ only in whether red cells are suspended in them, denies the factors in plasma and invents a cell-suspension split. Plasma is the post-clotting fluid, and serum is the fluid that still holds fibrinogen and the other factors, is the same reversal.

A.q: Hemoglobin, the pigment within red cells, is best described as which kind of substance?
options: A respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to a calcium compound.
A storage pigment built from a protein bound to an iron-protein compound.
A respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to an iron compound.
A visual pigment built from a protein bound to a retinal-protein compound.
A.explain: Hemoglobin is a respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to an iron compound. A respiratory pigment built from a protein bound to a calcium compound names the wrong metal. A storage pigment built from a protein bound to an iron-protein compound names the wrong pigment class. A visual pigment built from a protein bound to a retinal-protein compound is not the red-cell pigment.

A.q: Which statement correctly separates granulocytes from agranulocytes?
options: Granulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible cytoplasmic granules, while agranulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules.
Granulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules, while agranulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible cytoplasmic granules.
Granulocytes reside in the bone marrow, while agranulocytes reside in the lining of the small intestine.
Granulocytes manufacture antibodies, while agranulocytes perform phagocytosis of invading germs.
A.explain: Granulocytes are the polymorphonuclear leukocytes whose nuclei show several lobes and whose cytoplasm holds protein granules, namely neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Agranulocytes are the mononuclear leukocytes with one large nucleus, clear cytoplasm, and no granules, namely lymphocytes and monocytes. Granulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules, while agranulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible cytoplasmic granules, swaps the two definitions. Location in marrow versus gut does not define the split. Antibody production belongs to B lymphocytes, and phagocytosis is shared by neutrophils and monocytes, so that assignment misreads the classes.

A.q: A white cell whose granules stain neutral and that fights infection by phagocytosis, living about a day, is which type?
A.explain: The neutrophil is the granulocyte whose cytoplasmic granules take a neutral stain and that clears infection by phagocytosis, with a lifespan of up to about 24 hours. The eosinophil stains orange to rosy. The basophil stains dark blue. The monocyte also phagocytoses for about a day but is an agranulocyte with no granules.

A.q: Which white cell stains dark blue, takes part in immune surveillance, and releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue?
A.explain: The basophil is the short-lived granulocyte, usually under two days, that stains dark blue, contributes to immune surveillance, and brings anticoagulant substances to inflamed tissues. The neutrophil stains neutral. The eosinophil stains orange to rosy. The lymphocyte is an agranulocyte active in adaptive immunity.

A.q: Which white cell stains bright yellow-red to orange and increases during parasitic infection and allergic reactions?
A.explain: The eosinophil is the granulocyte that stains bright yellow-red, orange, or rosy and whose count rises during parasitic infections and allergic reactions, with a lifespan of about two to five days. The basophil stains dark blue. The neutrophil stains neutral. The monocyte is a non-granular phagocyte.

A.q: The word polymorphonuclear describes the granulocytes. Which reading of its parts is correct?
options: Poly means many, morpho means form, and nucleus means kernel, so the term refers to the many-lobed nucleus of these cells.
Poly means few, morpho means color, and nucleus means cell, so the term refers to the pale staining of these cells.
Poly means many, morpho means granule, and nucleus means sac, so the term refers to the granular cytoplasm of these cells.
Poly means one, morpho means form, and nucleus means center, so the term refers to the single round nucleus of these cells.
A.explain: In polymorphonuclear, poly means many, morpho means form, and nucleus means kernel, so the word describes the many-lobed nucleus of the granulocytes. Poly means few, morpho means color, and nucleus means cell misglosses the elements. Poly means many, morpho means granule, and nucleus means sac turns morpho into granule. Poly means one, morpho means form, and nucleus means center turns poly into one and describes a mononuclear cell.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign cells, cancer cells, and virus-infected cells?
options: The B-cell, which is bone-marrow derived and manufactures antibodies.
The T-cell, which is thymus dependent and carries out that attack.
The NK-cell, which carries cytotoxic substances against tumor cells.
The monocyte, which performs phagocytosis against germs in tissues.
A.explain: The T-cell is thymus dependent and carries out that attack on foreign cells, cancer cells, and virus-infected cells. The B-cell, which is bone-marrow derived and manufactures antibodies, makes antibody rather than attacking those cells. The NK-cell, which carries cytotoxic substances against tumor cells, kills through those substances and is not thymus dependent. The monocyte, which performs phagocytosis against germs in tissues, is a phagocyte, not that lymphocyte lineage.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte is bone-marrow derived and produces antibodies?
options: The T-cell, which matures under thymic influence.
The NK-cell, which contains cytotoxic substances.
The monocyte, which engulfs bacteria and fungi.
A.explain: The B-cell is bone-marrow derived, lives about five to six weeks, and makes antibodies against antigens. The T-cell, which matures under thymic influence, attacks cells directly. The NK-cell, which contains cytotoxic substances, kills through those substances. The monocyte, which engulfs bacteria and fungi, is a phagocytic agranulocyte rather than an antibody-producing lymphocyte.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte is a natural killer that destroys tumor or infected cells through cytotoxic substances?
options: The T-cell, which is thymus dependent.
The NK-cell, which carries the cytotoxic substances.
The neutrophil, which stains neutral and phagocytoses pathogens.
A.explain: The NK-cell, or natural killer cell, lives up to about two weeks and contains cytotoxic substances that can kill tumor or infected cells. The T-cell, which is thymus dependent, attacks cells but is not the natural killer class. The B-cell, which manufactures antibodies, makes antibody. The neutrophil, which stains neutral and phagocytoses pathogens, is a granulocyte rather than a lymphocyte.

A.q: Immunity, as a physiological mechanism, is best defined as the body's ability to do what?
options: Pump oxygenated blood to every tissue while returning deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
Recognize materials as foreign and neutralize, eliminate, or metabolize them without harming its own tissue.
Filter out old and damaged red cells and store the iron recovered from their breakdown.
Absorb dietary fats from the digestive tract and return them to the bloodstream.
A.explain: Immunity is the set of physiological mechanisms by which the body recognizes a material as foreign and then neutralizes, eliminates, or metabolizes it without injuring its own tissue. Pump oxygenated blood to every tissue while returning deoxygenated blood to the lungs is cardiac circulation. Filter out old and damaged red cells and store the iron recovered from their breakdown is a splenic function. Absorb dietary fats from the digestive tract and return them to the bloodstream is a lymphatic function.

A.q: Which pairing of term to definition is correct?
options: Antigen is a Y-shaped protein that destroys an invader, and antibody is the invader that triggers that protein.
Antigen and antibody are both foreign substances that enter the body from external sources.
Antigen is any substance that provokes antibody formation, and antibody is the Y-shaped protein that inactivates that antigen.
Antigen is the Y-shaped protein made by B cells, and antibody is the cytotoxic substance stored in natural killer cells.
A.explain: An antigen is any substance that, once introduced, causes the body to form antibody against it, and an antibody is the Y-shaped protein the body produces to destroy or inactivate that antigen. Antigen is a Y-shaped protein that destroys an invader, and antibody is the invader that triggers that protein, reverses the two roles. Antigen and antibody are both foreign substances that enter the body from external sources, treats the antibody as a foreign entrant. Antigen is the Y-shaped protein made by B cells, and antibody is the cytotoxic substance stored in natural killer cells, swaps both the shape and the cell of origin.

A.q: Which contrast between active and passive immunity is correct?
options: Active immunity is long-lasting and arises from the body making its own antibodies, while passive immunity is short-lasting and comes from antibodies received from elsewhere.
Active immunity is short-lived and supplied as foreign antibodies, while passive immunity is long-lived and built by the host's own antibody production.
Active immunity is long-lived yet supplied as foreign antibodies, while passive immunity is short-lived yet built by the host's own antibody production.
Active and passive immunity are equivalent short-lived states arising from the same placental transfer of maternal antibodies.
A.explain: Active immunity is long-lasting because the host is stimulated to produce its own antibodies, whereas passive immunity is short-lasting because it depends on foreign antibodies that are conveyed in and then degrade. Active immunity is short-lived and supplied as foreign antibodies, while passive immunity is long-lived and built by the host's own antibody production, swaps duration and mechanism. Active immunity is long-lived yet supplied as foreign antibodies, while passive immunity is short-lived yet built by the host's own antibody production, misattaches the duration. Active and passive immunity are equivalent short-lived states arising from the same placental transfer of maternal antibodies, equates the two and confines both to one passive route.

A.q: Within active immunity, how do the natural and artificial forms differ?
options: Natural active immunity follows a vaccine, while artificial active immunity follows a natural infection.
Natural active immunity is given as antiserum, while artificial active immunity is passed through breast milk.
Both natural and artificial active immunity are short-lived and rely on antibodies from another source.
Natural active immunity develops after an infection, while artificial active immunity develops after administration of a vaccine.
A.explain: Active immunity means the host makes its own antibodies. The natural route is recovery from an actual infection, and the artificial route is vaccination. Natural active immunity follows a vaccine, while artificial active immunity follows a natural infection, swaps the two labels. Natural active immunity is given as antiserum, while artificial active immunity is passed through breast milk, lists transfers of preformed antibody, which are passive. Both natural and artificial active immunity are short-lived and rely on antibodies from another source, calls active immunity short-lived and dependent on an outside source.

A.q: Within passive immunity, how do the natural and artificial forms differ?
options: Natural passive immunity follows a vaccine given to the host, while artificial passive immunity follows the host's recovery from a clinical infection.

Natural passive immunity passes from mother to fetus through the placenta and to the infant through breast milk, while artificial passive immunity is given as an injection of antibody-containing serum.
Natural passive immunity is built by the host after an exposure, while artificial passive immunity is built by the host after a vaccine dose.
Both natural and artificial passive immunity are long-lasting states created by the host's own memory cells after first contact.
A.explain: Passive immunity supplies preformed antibody. The natural route is maternal transfer across the placenta and through breast milk, and the artificial route is an injection of serum that already contains antibodies. Natural passive immunity follows a vaccine given to the host, while artificial passive immunity follows the host's recovery from a clinical infection, describes active immunity. Natural passive immunity is built by the host after an exposure, while artificial passive immunity is built by the host after a vaccine dose, also describes active immunity. Both natural and artificial passive immunity are long-lasting states created by the host's own memory cells after first contact, gives passive immunity the duration and memory of active immunity.

A.q: Which option lists pairs in which both members of every pair carry the same meaning?
options: Chrom/o with Splen/o; Hem/o with Thromb/o; Thym/o with Immun/o.
Chrom/o with Hem/o; Splen/o with Thromb/o; Lymph/o with Immun/o.
Chrom/o with Chromat/o; Hem/o with Hemat/o; Thym/o with Thym/i.
Chrom/o with Lymph/o; Hem/o with Splen/o; Thromb/o with Thym/o.
A.explain: Chrom/o and Chromat/o both mean color, Hem/o and Hemat/o both mean blood, and Thym/o and Thym/i both mean thymus. Chrom/o with Splen/o, Hem/o with Thromb/o, and Thym/o with Immun/o pairs color with spleen, blood with clot, and thymus with safe. Chrom/o with Hem/o, Splen/o with Thromb/o, and Lymph/o with Immun/o pairs color with blood, spleen with clot, and clear fluid with safe. Chrom/o with Lymph/o, Hem/o with Splen/o, and Thromb/o with Thym/o pairs color with clear fluid, blood with spleen, and clot with thymus.

A.q: In the term hemochromatosis, the element chrom refers to what?
A.explain: The term splits into hem/o meaning blood, chrom meaning color, and the suffix -osis meaning a condition, so chrom contributes the sense of color, as in the pigment or iron-color deposits of hemochromatosis. Blood is carried by the hem element of the same word. Clot and spleen belong to thromb/o and splen/o, which do not appear here.

A.q: In the term thrombophlebitis, the element thrombo refers to what?
A.explain: The term joins thrombo meaning clot, phleb meaning vein, and the suffix -itis meaning inflammation, so thrombo contributes the sense of clot. Vein is the phleb element of the same word. Color and blood belong to chrom/o and hem/o, neither of which is present.

A.q: In the term splenomegaly, the element spleno refers to what?
A.explain: The term combines spleno meaning spleen with the suffix -megaly meaning enlargement, so spleno names the spleen. Clot, thymus, and clear fluid are the senses of thromb/o, thym/o, and lymph/o.

A.q: In the term lymphoduct, the element lympho refers to what?
A.explain: Lympho is the combining form for the clear fluid lymph, so in lymphoduct it names that fluid and the term means a duct carrying lymph. Thymus, spleen, and color are the senses of thym/o, splen/o, and chrom/o.

A.q: In the term thymocyte, the element thymo refers to what?
A.explain: Thymo, with its variant thymi, is the combining form for the thymus, so in thymocyte it names that gland and the word means a cell of thymic origin. The same root shows in athymism, where the prefix a- denotes absence and thym still means thymus. Spleen, blood, and clot are the senses of splen/o, hem/o, and thromb/o.

A.q: What does the term hematocytopenia mean?
A.explain: Hematocytopenia is built from Hemat/o (blood), cyt/o (cell), and -penia (deficiency), so it denotes a deficiency of blood cells. An excess would use -osis or -cytosis, a platelet deficiency is thrombocytopenia, and clotting-factor excess is not the sense of this term.

A.q: What does the term splenomegaly mean?
A.explain: Splenomegaly is built from Splen/o (spleen) and -megaly (enlargement), so it denotes an enlarged spleen. Inflammation would use -itis, removal would use -ectomy, and pain would use -dynia.

A.q: What does the term thrombophlebitis mean?
options: Inflammation of an artery caused by a clot.
Inflammation of a vein caused by a clot.
Inflammation of the spleen caused by a clot.
Inflammation of the thymus caused by a clot.
A.explain: Thrombophlebitis is built from Thromb/o (clot), phleb (vein), and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a vein caused by a clot. Artery inflammation would use arteri/o, spleen inflammation would use Splen/o, and thymus inflammation would use Thym/o.

A.q: What does the term lymphoduct mean?
options: A duct that carries blood away from the heart.
A duct that carries lymph through the lymphatic system.
A duct that carries bile from the liver.
A duct that carries urine from the kidney.
A.explain: Lymphoduct is built from Lymph/o (lymph) and duct (a channel), so it denotes a duct that carries lymph through the lymphatic system. Blood vessels, bile ducts, and ureters are named by other combining forms and suffixes, such as vas/o, cholangi/o, and ureter/o.

A.q: What does the term thymocyte mean?
options: A cell of the bone marrow.
A cell of the lymph node.
A.explain: Thymocyte is built from Thym/o (thymus) and -cyte (cell), so it denotes a cell of the thymus. Spleen cells would use Splen/o, bone marrow cells would use Myel/o, and lymph node cells would use Lymph/o.

A.q: What does the term athymism mean?
A.explain: Athymism is built from the prefix a- (without), Thym/o (thymus), and -ism (condition), so it denotes the absence of the thymus. Enlargement would use -megaly, inflammation would use -itis, and surgical removal would use -ectomy.

A.q: What does the term immunopharmacology mean?
options: The study of drugs that act on the immune system.
The study of drugs that act on the heart.
The study of drugs that act on the kidneys.
The study of drugs that act on the lungs.
A.explain: Immunopharmacology is built from Immun/o (safe, immune), pharmac/o (drug), and -logy (study), so it denotes the study of drugs that act on the immune system. The other options would use cardi/o, nephr/o, and pulmon/o respectively, none of which appears in this term.

A.q: What does the term hemochromatosis mean?
options: A condition of excess blood cells.
A condition involving excessive iron deposits and skin color changes.
A condition of deficient blood clotting.
A condition of excess clots in the veins.
A.explain: Hemochromatosis is built from Hem/o (blood), chromat/o (color), and -osis (condition), so it denotes a condition involving excessive iron deposits and the resulting skin color changes. Excess blood cells would use -cytosis, deficient clotting would use a different suffix, and excess clots in veins is thrombophlebitis.

A.q: Which structure is the lymphoid organ that produces T-lymphocytes to fight off foreign organisms?
A.explain: The thymus produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms. The spleen filters old blood cells, the tonsils trap pathogens from food and air, and the appendix helps house good bacteria.

A.q: Which structure filters and removes old and damaged blood cells and fights infection and disease?
A.explain: The spleen filters and removes old and damaged blood cells and fights infection and disease. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the bone marrow produces blood cells, and the Peyer's patches monitor and destroy bacteria in the small intestine.

A.q: Which structures trap pathogens from food and air and act as the first line of defense against foreign invaders?
options: The Peyer's patches and lymph nodes.
A.explain: The tonsils and adenoid trap pathogens from food and air and act as the first line of defense against foreign invaders. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters blood cells, the bone marrow produces blood cells, the appendix houses good bacteria, and the Peyer's patches monitor bacteria in the small intestine.

A.q: Which structure produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets?
A.explain: The bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters old blood cells, and the tonsils trap pathogens.

A.q: Which structures are found in the lining of the small intestine and monitor and destroy bacteria?
A.explain: The Peyer's patches are found in the lining of the small intestine and monitor and destroy bacteria. The tonsils and adenoids trap pathogens from food and air, and the appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria.

A.q: Which structure plays a role in housing good bacteria?
A.explain: The appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters old blood cells, and the tonsils trap pathogens from food and air.

A.q: Which fluid is the colorless, watery liquid collected from the body tissues and moved back into the bloodstream by the lymphatic system?
A.explain: Lymph is the colorless, watery fluid collected from the body tissues and moved back into the circulatory system by the lymphatic network. Plasma and serum are blood fractions, and interstitial fluid is the tissue fluid before it enters the lymphatic capillaries.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between interstitial fluid and lymph?
options: Interstitial fluid is the fluid inside blood vessels, and lymph is the fluid inside lymphatic vessels.
Interstitial fluid is the fluid between tissue cells, and lymph is the fluid once it has entered the lymphatic capillaries.
Interstitial fluid is the fluid inside the cells, and lymph is the fluid inside the bone marrow.
Interstitial fluid is the fluid in the thoracic duct, and lymph is the fluid in the blood capillaries.
A.explain: Interstitial fluid is the fluid that bathes the tissue cells, and once it enters the lymphatic capillaries it is called lymph. Interstitial fluid is the fluid inside blood vessels, and lymph is the fluid inside lymphatic vessels, reverses the two. Interstitial fluid is the fluid inside the cells, and lymph is the fluid inside the bone marrow, places them inside cells and marrow. Interstitial fluid is the fluid in the thoracic duct, and lymph is the fluid in the blood capillaries, reverses the ducts and capillaries.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the function of valves in the lymphatic vessels?
options: They prevent lymph from flowing backward and help keep it moving toward the bloodstream.
They filter microorganisms and foreign particles out of the lymph as it passes.
They produce lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms in the lymph.
They store old and damaged blood cells until they can be removed.
A.explain: Valves in the lymphatic vessels prevent backflow and help keep lymph moving toward the bloodstream. Filtration of microorganisms is a function of the lymph nodes, lymphocyte production occurs in the thymus and bone marrow, and blood cell storage is a splenic function.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the flow of lymph through a lymph node?
options: Lymph enters through the efferent vessel and leaves through the afferent vessel.
Lymph enters through the afferent vessel and leaves through the efferent vessel.
Lymph enters through the artery and leaves through the vein.
Lymph enters through the thoracic duct and leaves through the right lymphatic duct.
A.explain: Lymph enters a lymph node through the afferent lymphatic vessel and leaves through the efferent lymphatic vessel. Lymph enters through the efferent vessel and leaves through the afferent vessel, reverses the two. Lymph enters through the artery and leaves through the vein, confuses lymph vessels with blood vessels. Lymph enters through the thoracic duct and leaves through the right lymphatic duct, names the two main lymphatic trunks rather than the vessels of a single node.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes how lymph is returned to the bloodstream?
options: Lymph is collected by lymphatic capillaries, filtered through lymph nodes, and returned to the bloodstream through the lymphatic trunks and ducts.
Lymph is collected by the arteries, filtered through the spleen, and returned to the bloodstream through the veins.
Lymph is produced in the bone marrow, filtered through the thymus, and returned to the bloodstream through the heart.
Lymph is produced in the tonsils, filtered through the appendix, and returned to the bloodstream through the lungs.
A.explain: Lymph is collected by the lymphatic capillaries, filtered through the lymph nodes, and returned to the bloodstream through the lymphatic trunks and ducts. Lymph is collected by the arteries, filtered through the spleen, and returned to the bloodstream through the veins, assigns the path to blood vessels and the spleen. Lymph is produced in the bone marrow, filtered through the thymus, and returned to the bloodstream through the heart, assigns it to marrow, thymus, and heart. Lymph is produced in the tonsils, filtered through the appendix, and returned to the bloodstream through the lungs, assigns it to tonsils, appendix, and lungs.

A.q: Match each type of blood cell to the feature that defines it.

rightItems.text: Granulocyte with neutral-staining granules that phagocytoses pathogens and lives about a day
Cell fragment shed from megakaryocytes that is essential for coagulation
Respiratory carrier of oxygen and carbon dioxide with a lifespan of about 110 to 120 days
Granulocyte with dark blue granules that releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue
Agranulocyte with a single large nucleus that phagocytoses germs and infected cells
Granulocyte with orange to rosy granules that rises in parasitic and allergic states

A.explain: The erythrocyte is the respiratory carrier with a lifespan of about 110 to 120 days. The neutrophil is the granulocyte whose granules stain neutral and that phagocytoses pathogens with a lifespan up to about 24 hours. The basophil is the granulocyte with dark blue granules that releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue. The eosinophil is the granulocyte with orange to rosy granules that rises in parasitic and allergic states. The monocyte is the agranulocyte with a single large nucleus that phagocytoses germs. The thrombocyte is the cell fragment shed from megakaryocytes that is essential for coagulation. Each feature is phrased so that the cell must be identified by its granule stain, lifespan, or role rather than by a repeated name.

A.q: Match each type of lymphocyte to the feature that defines it.

rightItems.text: Matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign, cancerous, and virus-infected cells.
Arises in the bone marrow and manufactures antibodies against antigens.
Acts as a natural killer carrying cytotoxic substances that destroy tumor or infected cells.

A.explain: T-cells are thymus-dependent and target foreign, cancerous, and virus-infected cells, living about 30 to 160 days, so they match the thymic-influence feature. B-cells are bone-marrow derived and produce antibodies, living about five to six weeks, so they match the antibody-manufacturing feature. NK-cells are natural killers holding cytotoxic substances that destroy tumor or infected cells, living up to about two weeks, so they match the cytotoxic feature. The three lineages are distinguished by their site of maturation and their effector mechanism, not by granule content, since all are agranulocytes.

A.q: Match each lymphatic organ to the role it performs.

rightItems.text: Houses beneficial bacteria.
Generates T-lymphocytes that combat foreign organisms.
Filters out and removes aged or damaged blood cells and fights infection.
Forms red cells, white cells, and platelets.
Traps pathogens from food and air as a first line of defense.
Monitors and destroys bacteria along the small intestine.

A.explain: The thymus produces the T-lymphocytes that fight foreign organisms, the spleen filters and removes old and damaged blood cells while resisting infection, the tonsils and adenoids trap pathogens from food and air as a first line of defense, the bone marrow is the source of red cells, white cells, and platelets, the Peyer's patches sit in the wall of the small intestine to monitor and destroy bacteria, and the appendix helps house good bacteria. Each organ is fixed to its own role by what it makes or what it filters, so the pairing follows the function rather than the position in the body.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.

rightItems.text: Blood
Clot
Color
Safe
Clear fluid
Spleen

A.explain: Chrom/o and Chromat/o both mean color, as in hemochromatosis, Hem/o and Hemat/o both mean blood, as in hematocytopenia, Splen/o means spleen, as in splenomegaly, Thromb/o means clot, as in thrombophlebitis, Immun/o means safe, as in immunopharmacology, and Lymph/o means the clear fluid lymph, as in lymphoduct. The remaining form of this group, Thym/o with Thym/i, means thymus, as in thymocyte and athymism.

A.q: Match each term to its meaning.

rightItems.text: Inflammation of a vein caused by a clot.
A deficiency of blood cells.
A cell of the thymus.
Enlargement of the spleen.
Absence of the thymus.
A duct that carries lymph.

A.explain: Hematocytopenia is a deficiency of blood cells. Splenomegaly is enlargement of the spleen. Thrombophlebitis is inflammation of a vein caused by a clot. Lymphoduct is a duct that carries lymph. Thymocyte is a cell of the thymus. Athymism is absence of the thymus. Each term is built from the combining forms and suffixes of this unit, and the meaning follows directly from those elements.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the lymph nodes in the lymphatic system?
options: They filter microorganisms and foreign particles from the lymph as it passes through.
They produce red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
They manufacture antibodies and release them into the bloodstream.
They store old and damaged red blood cells until they can be removed.
A.explain: The lymph nodes filter microorganisms and foreign particles from the lymph as it passes through, which is a key part of the lymphatic system's protective role. Blood cell production is a bone marrow function, antibody manufacture is a B-cell function, and storage of old red cells is a splenic function.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of lymphatic capillaries?
options: They carry blood away from the heart under pressure.
They collect interstitial fluid from the tissues and begin its return to the bloodstream.
They produce T-lymphocytes that fight foreign organisms.
They store old and damaged blood cells until they can be removed.
A.explain: Lymphatic capillaries collect interstitial fluid from the tissues and begin its return to the bloodstream as lymph. Carrying blood away from the heart is an arterial function, T-lymphocyte production is a thymic function, and storage of old blood cells is a splenic function.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the thoracic duct in the lymphatic system?
options: It collects lymph from the lower body and the left side of the head and chest and returns it to the bloodstream.
It collects lymph from the right side of the head and chest and returns it to the bloodstream.
It filters microorganisms and foreign particles from the lymph as it passes through.
It produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
